title: Carcinization Strikes Again: New Study Traces the Crab Shape’s Repeated Evolution
summary: If you’ve spent any time on the internet, you’ve probably encountered the meme: “Everything eventually evolves into a crab.” It’s a playful exaggeration, but the underlying science — carcinization — is very real. The term, coined by zoologist Lancelot Alexander Borradaile in 1916, describes the tendency of diverse crustacean lineages to converge on a crab-like body plan: a flattened, wide carapace with a tucked-under abdomen. Now, a new eLife-reviewed preprint on true crabs (Brachyura) suggests that the iconic sideways walk evolved just once, from a forward-moving ancestor, near the base of a group called Eubrachyura. But the crab shape itself? That’s a different story. It has appeared independently in several anomuran crustaceans — the group that includes hermit crabs, king crabs, and squat lobsters. A 2017 paper in the Biological Journal of the Linnean Society highlighted how king crabs, for instance, evolved from hermit crab ancestors, re-evolving a hardened, symmetrical body. The new research adds locomotion data and genomic analysis to the puzzle. A January 2026 study in Animal Cells and Systems analyzed 42 anomuran mitochondrial genomes and placed key divergence events around the Eocene-Oligocene transition, a period of dramatic climate change that may have driven adaptation. Meanwhile, a February 2026 paper in the Journal of Crustacean Biology benchmarked the decapod fossil record at 4,225 species, finding diversity peaks in the Late Jurassic, Late Cretaceous, Eocene, and Miocene — eras when crab-like forms flourished. So why crabs? The shape offers advantages for hiding in crevices and scuttling along the seafloor. But as the 2017 paper noted, internal anatomy doesn’t always match the external form; nervous and circulatory systems can vary widely between crab-like lineages. Carcinization isn’t a destiny — it’s a repeated evolutionary solution to a common set of problems. And it’s a reminder that nature loves a good remix.
why_it_matters: Carcinization isn't just a quirky fact—it's a powerful illustration of convergent evolution, showing that under similar pressures, life can repeatedly arrive at the same solution. For young people, this connects internet culture with real science, and it highlights how understanding evolution helps us predict how species might adapt to a changing world, including our oceans.

background_read: The idea that 'everything eventually evolves into a crab' is a popular internet meme, but it is rooted in real biology. In 1916, British zoologist Lancelot Alexander Borradaile coined the term 'carcinization' to describe how many crustaceans—not just true crabs—independently evolve a crab-like body: a wide, flattened shell with a small tail tucked underneath. This is a classic example of convergent evolution, where unrelated organisms develop similar traits because they face similar environmental challenges.

True crabs belong to a group called Brachyura, which appeared in the fossil record over 150 million years ago. However, other decapod crustaceans that are not 'true crabs'—such as king crabs, hermit crabs, and squat lobsters (all part of a group called Anomura)—have also repeatedly hit on the crab body plan. A 2017 study showed that king crabs evolved from hermit crab ancestors, re-evolving a hard, symmetrical shell millions of years after their lineage had lost it.

Scientists now use modern genomic techniques and extensive fossil databases to track when and why these transformations happened. The new studies tie some key crab-like shifts to periods of climate upheaval, like a sudden cooling near the Eocene-Oligocene boundary, which may have favored the hiding and scuttling lifestyle that a crab-shape enables.
Article_Structure: LEAD: The internet meme 'everything evolves into a crab' has scientific truth—called carcinization—as an example of repeated convergent evolution.
HISTORY OF THE TERM: Coined in 1916 by zoologist Lancelot Alexander Borradaile.
├─ TRUE CRABS (Brachyura): Sideways walk evolved only once, from a forward-moving ancestor.
└─ CRAB SHAPE, HOWEVER: Has appeared independently many times in anomuran crustaceans (hermit crabs, king crabs, squat lobsters).
├─ A 2017 paper detailed how king crabs re-evolved a hardened, symmetrical shell from hermit crab ancestors.
├─ A January 2026 mitochondrial genome study linked major divergences to the Eocene-Oligocene climate transition.
└─ A February 2026 fossil record analysis benchmarked 4,225 decapod species, finding diversity peaks in eras when crab-like forms flourished.
WHY THE CRAB SHAPE? It offers advantages for hiding in crevices and moving efficiently along the seafloor, though internal anatomy can vary widely.
CONCLUSION: Carcinization is not a destiny—it's a repeated evolutionary solution to common environmental problems, showing that nature loves a good remix.

perspectives.description: The crab shape is a brilliant adaptation for life on the seafloor, allowing creatures to slip into cracks and scuttle efficiently. The fact that evolution has landed on this body plan again and again suggests it's a remarkably effective solution—an example of nature's ingenuity at its best.

Some scientists warn that the meme overstates the case. Not all crustaceans are marching toward crabhood; many cling to shrimp-like or lobster-like forms, and the detailed internal anatomy of 'crab-like' groups can be very different. Treating carcinization as a rule risks obscuring the messy, branching reality of evolution.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral/analytical: A window into deep time
perspectives.description: By combining genomics and the fossil record, researchers can pinpoint when and under what conditions crab-like forms emerged. This approach shows that convergence often coincides with major environmental shifts, offering insights into how life on Earth responds to climate and ecological crises over millions of years.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking: What can we learn about adaptation?
perspectives.description: As oceans warm and coastal habitats change, understanding why certain body plans succeed could help predict which species are more resilient. Future studies might even reveal whether other animal groups are on their own 'carcinization-like' paths, guiding conservation efforts in a rapidly transforming world.
